questions.q: What is the precise definition of an entangled multi-qubit state?
options: A state whose qubits are physically touching each other
A state that cannot be written as a tensor product of individual single-qubit states
Any state with more than one term in its superposition
A state that was created using a Hadamard gate
questions.explain: Entanglement is defined precisely as non-factorizability: there is no way to express the joint state as (single-qubit state) ⊗ (single-qubit state). Having multiple terms or using specific gates doesn't by itself make a state entangled — |+⟩⊗|+⟩ has four terms and is still a product state.

questions.q: The state |+⟩⊗|+⟩ = (|00⟩+|01⟩+|10⟩+|11⟩)/2 is NOT entangled. Why not, even though it has four terms in its superposition?
options: Because it isn't normalized
Because it has exactly four terms, and entangled states always have fewer
Because it was explicitly constructed as a tensor product of two independent |+⟩ states, so it factors by definition
Because measuring qubit 1 always gives the same result as measuring qubit 2
questions.explain: It's written right in its construction: |+⟩⊗|+⟩ is explicitly the tensor product of two independent single-qubit |+⟩ states, so it trivially factors. It is normalized (4 × 0.25 = 1), and the number of terms in a superposition has no bearing on factorizability — what matters is whether a valid product decomposition exists.

questions.q: In the proof that |Φ+⟩ = (|00⟩+|11⟩)/√2 cannot be factored, assuming |Φ+⟩ = (a|0⟩+b|1⟩)⊗(c|0⟩+d|1⟩) leads to which contradiction?
options: The resulting state would not be normalized
ac and bd must both be nonzero (equal to 1/√2), yet ad=0 and bc=0 simultaneously require one of a, b, c, or d to be zero — which would force ac or bd to also be zero
a, b, c, and d would all have to be negative
The equations would have infinitely many valid solutions
questions.explain: Matching coefficients requires ac=1/√2, bd=1/√2, ad=0, and bc=0. Since ac and bd are nonzero, none of a, b, c, d can individually be zero — but ad=0 and bc=0 both demand that one of them IS zero. That's the contradiction: no consistent values exist.

questions.q: If you measure qubit 1 of the product state |+⟩⊗|+⟩ and get the result 0, what does that tell you about qubit 2?
options: Qubit 2 is now also guaranteed to measure 0
Qubit 2 is now guaranteed to measure 1
Nothing new — qubit 2 was already independently 50/50, unaffected by what happened to qubit 1
Qubit 2 collapses to a mixture of |+⟩ and |−⟩
questions.explain: Because the state factors into two independent qubits, measuring one has no effect on the other's statistics. Qubit 2 remains 50/50 on 0 or 1, exactly as it was before qubit 1 was measured. This is the key behavioral difference from an entangled state like |Φ+⟩.

questions.q: Why does the non-factorizability of a state like |Φ+⟩ matter for quantum computing and cryptography, beyond being a mathematical curiosity?
options: It doesn't matter in practice — it's purely a notational detail

It means the two qubits no longer have individual states of their own; only the joint pair has a well-defined description, which is the actual resource later algorithms, teleportation, and device-independent cryptography protocols exploit
It only matters because entangled qubits must be physically adjacent on the chip
It matters only for error correction, not for algorithms or cryptography
questions.explain: Non-factorizability means the pair carries information and correlation that cannot be decomposed into two separate single-qubit descriptions. That irreducibly joint structure is what algorithms, quantum teleportation (chapter 5), and device-independent QKD (lesson 19) actually rely on.
